title: Word Equations, Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Chemistry
summary: How to write word equations and name the products, the main reaction patterns, and how to use a temperature change to decide whether a reaction or process is exothermic or endothermic.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Use word equations to describe chemical reactions. (8Cc.01)
Know that some processes and reactions are endothermic or exothermic, and that you can tell which by measuring the temperature change. (8Cc.02)

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: reactant
مادة متفاعلة — a substance you start with
product
ناتج — a new substance made in the reaction
word equation
معادلة لفظية — a reaction written with the names of the substances
salt
ملح — a compound made when an acid reacts; e.g. copper sulfate
combustion
احتراق — burning a fuel in oxygen
exothermic
طارد للحرارة — gives out energy to the surroundings; temperature rises
endothermic
ماص للحرارة — takes in energy from the surroundings; temperature falls
surroundings
الوسط المحيط — everything around the reaction: the solution, the container, the air, your hand
temperature change
التغير في درجة الحرارة — final temperature − starting temperature
insulate
يعزل — stop heat moving in or out

blocks.text: 2. Writing a word equation
In a chemical reaction new substances are made. A **word equation** shows this using names only.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 540 135" width="540" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13"><text x="270" y="50" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" font-weight="bold">magnesium  +  oxygen  →  magnesium oxide</text><path d="M62 62 q0 10 10 10 L150 72 q10 0 10 10 q0 -10 10 -10 L250 72 q10 0 10 -10" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="160" y="102" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">reactants</text><text x="160" y="120" text-anchor="middle">(what you start with)</text><path d="M330 62 q0 10 10 10 L390 72 q10 0 10 10 q0 -10 10 -10 L470 72 q10 0 10 -10" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="400" y="102" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">product</text><text x="400" y="120" text-anchor="middle">(the new substance made)</text><text x="300" y="22" text-anchor="middle">arrow = "reacts to make"</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Parts of a word equation.

items: Write the **reactants** on the left, joined by **+**.
Draw an **arrow** (→). It means "react to make". **Never** use an equals sign (=).
Write the **products** on the right, joined by **+**.
**Check:** every element in the reactants must also appear somewhere in the products — atoms are not made or destroyed, just rearranged.

blocks.title: The element check
blocks.text: In "magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide" the elements magnesium and oxygen are on both sides. If you wrote "magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide + hydrogen", the hydrogen would come from nowhere — so it must be wrong. This check catches many mistakes.

blocks.alt: A strip of magnesium ribbon burning with a very bright white flame
blocks.caption: Magnesium burning in air with a dazzling white flame. The white powder and smoke are magnesium oxide: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide (an exothermic reaction).
blocks.credit: Photo: Capt. John Yossarian / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: 3. Naming the products

**Two elements joined** — the metal keeps its name and the non-metal ends in **-ide**: oxygen → oxide, chlorine → chloride, sulfur → sulfide. So iron + sulfur → **iron sulfide**; sodium + chlorine → **sodium chloride**.
**Names ending in -ate** contain **oxygen** as well: copper **carbonate** contains copper, carbon and oxygen; zinc **sulfate** contains zinc, sulfur and oxygen.
**Salts from acids.** When an acid reacts, the product called a **salt** takes its first name from the metal and its second name from the acid:

rows: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen
copper oxide + nitric acid → copper nitrate + water

blocks.text: 4. Reaction patterns to learn
Most reactions you meet at Stage 8 follow a small number of patterns. Learn the pattern and you can write the word equation for any metal or acid.

rows: iron + hydrochloric acid → iron chloride + hydrogen
hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water
copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water
carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide
calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide

blocks.alt: A small pile of green copper carbonate powder
blocks.caption: Copper carbonate is a green powder. When it is heated strongly it breaks down into black copper oxide and carbon dioxide — a thermal decomposition.
blocks.credit: Photo: Metabisulfite / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: **From a description to an equation.** Read the question and underline the substances. Those you **start with** (or that are **added** or **used up**) are reactants; those that are **made**, **formed** or **given off** are products. Air or burning means **oxygen** is a reactant even if the question does not say it.

blocks.title: قاعدة المعادلة اللفظية
blocks.text: المواد المتفاعلة (reactants) على الشمال، والنواتج (products) على اليمين، وبينهم سهم → مش علامة يساوي. أي عنصر موجود في الشمال لازم يكون موجود في اليمين. أسماء الأملاح: hydrochloric ← chloride، sulfuric ← sulfate، nitric ← nitrate. فلز + أكسجين ← أكسيد الفلز. فلز + حمض ← ملح + هيدروجين.
5. Exothermic and endothermic changes

Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. Energy (usually as heat) moves **between the chemicals and their surroundings**. The surroundings are everything around the reacting particles — the water they are dissolved in, the container, the thermometer, the air, your hand.

rows: burning fuels; respiration; neutralisation; metals with acids; iron rusting (very slowly); iron powder in hand warmers
citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate (the cold fizz in sherbet); thermal decomposition (needs heat all the time); photosynthesis (takes in light energy)
condensing; freezing; dissolving some solids, e.g. calcium chloride
melting; evaporating and boiling; dissolving some solids, e.g. ammonium nitrate (used in instant cold packs)

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: **EX**othermic = energy **EX**its (leaves) → hotter. **EN**dothermic = energy **EN**ters → colder.
6. Identifying the type from a temperature change

items: Measure the **starting temperature** of the reactants with a thermometer.
Mix the reactants (stir) and watch the thermometer.
Record the **highest** temperature (if it rises) or the **lowest** temperature (if it falls).
Work out **temperature change = final temperature − starting temperature**.
A **rise** means **exothermic**; a **fall** means **endothermic**.

blocks.text: **Making it accurate and fair:** use a **polystyrene cup** with a lid — polystyrene is a good thermal insulator, so less energy escapes to or comes in from the room. Use the **same volume** of liquid and the **same mass** of solid each time, start at the **same temperature**, and **repeat** to check your results. Wear eye protection when using acids.
**Reading a thermometer:** read at eye level and work out what each small division is worth before you read it (for example, if there are 10 divisions between 20 °C and 30 °C, each is 1 °C).
7. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — When sodium burns in chlorine, sodium chloride is made. Write the word equation. [1]

items: Reactants (start): sodium and chlorine. Product (made): sodium chloride.
**sodium + chlorine → sodium chloride**
Element check: sodium ✓, chlorine ✓ on both sides.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Complete the word equation: magnesium + sulfuric acid → __________ + __________ [2]

items: Pattern: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
Salt: metal name **magnesium** + sulfuric → **sulfate** = **magnesium sulfate** (1).
Other product: **hydrogen** (1).
**Common mistake:** "magnesium sulfuric" or "magnesium sulfide". Sulfuric acid always gives a **sulfate**.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Copper carbonate is a green powder. When it is heated it turns black (copper oxide) and a gas that turns limewater milky is given off. Write the word equation. [2]

items: The gas that turns limewater milky is **carbon dioxide**.
**copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide** (1 for the reactant, 1 for both products).
Only one reactant here: heat is the **condition**, not a substance, so it is **not** written as a reactant (you may write "heat" above the arrow).

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to hydrochloric acid. The temperature goes from 22 °C to 31 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature change. [1] (b) Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Explain. [2]

items: (b) **Exothermic** (1) — the temperature **rose**, so energy was **given out** to the surroundings (1).
**Common mistake:** writing "the reaction took in heat so it got hotter". Getting hotter means energy came **out** of the reacting chemicals.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water. The temperature falls from 20 °C to 13 °C. (a) Is dissolving ammonium nitrate exothermic or endothermic? [1] (b) Suggest a use for this. [1] (c) Why is it called a **process** here, not a reaction? [1]

items: (a) **Endothermic** — the temperature fell by 7 °C.
(b) An instant **cold pack** for sports injuries.
(c) Dissolving is a physical change: **no new substance** is made (the solid can be got back by evaporating the water).

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Mariam tests four solids dissolving in water. Her results are in the table. Which solids dissolve exothermically? [2]

items: Work out each change: A +7, B −4, C 0, D +13.
Rises = exothermic: **A and D** (1 mark each).
C shows no change — neither exothermic nor endothermic (or too small to measure).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Using "=" instead of "→", or writing "and" instead of "+".
Forgetting **oxygen** as a reactant when something burns.
Writing "heat" as a reactant or product — heat is energy, not a substance.
Naming salts wrongly: sulfuric → **sulfate**, hydrochloric → **chloride**, nitric → **nitrate**.
Getting exothermic and endothermic backwards: exothermic **feels hot** because energy is given **out** to you.
Subtracting the wrong way and giving a negative "rise". Say clearly whether the temperature **rose** or **fell**, and by how much.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Complete** a word equation with one or two missing names.
**Write** a full word equation from a description (reactants, arrow, products).
**Read thermometers** before and after, **calculate** the change and **state** exothermic or endothermic with a reason.
**Read a temperature–time graph**: lowest/highest temperature, size of the change.
**Classify** processes (melting, freezing, burning, dissolving) as exothermic or endothermic.
**Plan** a fair test: polystyrene cup, measured volumes and masses, starting temperature, repeat.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Word equations and energy changes — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: In a word equation, where are the **reactants** written?
c: to the left of the arrow
to the right of the arrow
questions.e: Reactants (the starting substances) go on the **left** of the arrow; products (the new substances) go on the right.

questions.q:
Complete the word equation.
magnesium + oxygen → ______________
questions.e: A metal burning in oxygen makes the metal **oxide**: magnesium + oxygen → **magnesium oxide**. (Not "magnesium oxygen" — two elements joined make an "-ide".)

questions.q:
Complete the word equation.
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + ______________
questions.e: metal + acid → salt + **hydrogen**. Zinc chloride is the salt; the gas given off is hydrogen (it gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint).

questions.q:
Complete the word equation.
copper oxide + sulfuric acid → ______________ + water
questions.e: metal oxide + acid → salt + water. The metal (copper) gives the first name; **sulfuric** acid makes **sulfates**. So the salt is **copper sulfate**.

questions.q: Methane is the main gas in natural gas. Which word equation shows methane burning completely in air?
questions.e: Burning (combustion) needs **oxygen**. Methane contains carbon and hydrogen; the carbon makes **carbon dioxide** and the hydrogen makes **water**. Check: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen appear on both sides.

questions.q: (b) What type of reaction is this, and why?
c: endothermic, because energy was given out
questions.e: The temperature **rose**, so energy was **given out** to the surroundings (the solution and thermometer): the reaction is **exothermic**.

questions.q: (c) Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic?
questions.e: The temperature **fell**, so the reaction took in energy from the surroundings: **endothermic**. After 3 minutes the reaction had finished and the cold mixture slowly warmed up again by taking energy from the warmer room — that part is not the reaction.

Melting **takes in** energy from the surroundings (ice cools your drink as it melts), so it is endothermic. Burning is exothermic; condensing and freezing **give out** energy, so they are exothermic too.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid. Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide are made. Write the word equation for this reaction. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: reactants calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid on the left of an arrow. 1 mark: products calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide on the right (any order). Do not award the second mark if '=' is used instead of an arrow or if 'and' replaces every '+'. Ignore state symbols.
questions.e: **calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide**. This is the carbonate + acid pattern: salt + water + carbon dioxide (the fizzing gas).

questions.q: Plan an experiment to find out whether dissolving a white solid in water is exothermic or endothermic. Include the equipment, what you measure and how you decide. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: measure a fixed volume of water (measuring cylinder) into an insulated container (polystyrene cup), and measure its starting temperature with a thermometer. 1 mark: add a measured mass of the solid (balance), stir, and record the highest/lowest/final temperature. 1 mark: temperature rises = exothermic; temperature falls = endothermic. Accept any sensible control (same volume of water / same starting temperature) or repeating as part of the first two marks.
questions.e: Pour 50 cm³ of water into a polystyrene cup (it insulates) and record the temperature. Add 5 g of the solid, stir, and record the temperature once it stops changing (the highest or lowest reading). Work out final − starting temperature. If the temperature **rose**, dissolving is **exothermic**; if it **fell**, it is **endothermic**. Repeat to check the result.

questions.q: A hand warmer contains iron powder. When the packet is opened, the iron reacts with oxygen from the air. Explain why the hand warmer feels warm. Use the word **exothermic** in your answer. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the reaction (iron + oxygen) is exothermic. 1 mark: it gives out/transfers (heat) energy to the surroundings / to your hands, so the temperature rises. Do not accept 'it makes heat' alone for the second mark without the idea of transfer to the surroundings/hand.
questions.e: The reaction of iron with oxygen is **exothermic**: it **gives out energy** (as heat) to its surroundings. Your hands are part of the surroundings, so they warm up. (Word equation: iron + oxygen → iron oxide.)

blocks.title: Remember
items: Word equation: reactants → products, with + between substances and an arrow, never =.
Patterns: metal + oxygen → metal oxide; metal + acid → salt + hydrogen; carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide; fuel + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Salt names: chloride (hydrochloric), sulfate (sulfuric), nitrate (nitric).
Exothermic: energy given out, temperature rises. Endothermic: energy taken in, temperature falls.
Temperature change = final − starting temperature; use an insulated cup and repeat for reliable results.
